This is important in ensuring glycolysis only occurs when there is enough energy in the cell - it's a safety mechanism to prevent energetic collapse of the cell. The biliary tree, proximal duodenum, sigmoid colon and distal 1/3rd of transverse colon are all supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery. The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, which comprises the oesophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, biliary tree and part of the pancreas. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, which comprises the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum and appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3rds of the transverse colon and part of the pancreas. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut, which comprises the distal 1/3rd of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, proximal anal canal and rectum. Embryologically the midgut follows the superior mesenteric artery, the hindgut follows the inferior mesenteric artery and the foregut follows the coeliac trunk. This answer is therefore C - the appendix extends from the posteromedial aspect of the caecum, which in turn is supplied by the sup mesenteric artery. This area is also known as the posterior visceral pocket and is one of two areas (the other being the anterior visceral pocket, which is supplied by the infracolic trunk) where the solid organs are vulnerable to damage. Most of the large intestine is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, with the exception of the distal 1/3rd of the transverse colon, which is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. Virchow's Triad states that:That thrombosis occurs due to alteration in:The integrity of the vessel wallThe composition of the blood to render it hyper-coagulativeBlood flow. Myocardial Infarctions, when a result of a ruptured plaque, are a classic example of a disease process that results in a change of the three tenets in Virchow's Triad. The integrity of the vessel wall has been compromised by the rupture of the plaque; the composition of the blood has been altered by exposure to the thrombogenic contents of the plaque and there is reduced blood flow due to the narrowing caused by the plaque. Atherslerotic plaques themselves are result of a change in one or more of the tenets of Virchow's Triad. And so atherosclerosis could be considered as the primary disease process, with the rupture of the plaque causing a myocardial infarction. In this case, the principle behind Virchow's Triad could be applied to a range of disease processes resulting in a change in the three tenets. However, it is most commonly used to explain the aetiology of myocardial infarctions.  Other possible disease processes which could be said to result in a change in the three tenets of Virchow's Triad include:Cerebral emboliClopidogrel-induced platelet inhibition & bleedingCardioembolismCirculatory collapse from severe hypovolaemiaDisruption of anticoagulant therapy - e.g. warfarinDamage to vessel walls from repetitive invasive procedures - chronic CV diseaseHaemophiliaAtherosclerosis is a chronic disease process. Adenosine is a sleep inducing molecule that is liberated during the breakdown of ATP. It binds to adenosine receptors and causes them to fire more slowly, making you sleepy. As it is a receptor agonist, it induces sleep. As soon as adenosine is released, it is quickly followed by the release of glucagon which keeps you awake. Hence, if you want to induce sleep you need to cover up the function of adenosine receptors so that they are inactive. This is done by caffeine, which is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and, consequently, leads to the uptake of adenosine without allowing it to fire the adenosine receptors. Because glucagon is being secreted, you are then awake. When you switch off the caffeine (i.e. when the blood concentration decreases), the adenosine receptors become uncovered and start firing, inducing sleep. For this reason, you should never ask someone whether they want coffee or tea, because they will always say coffee! (The stimulant that keeps you awake longer will also disrupt your adenosine even more.) Case 10 - plenary - sleep. More information in the PCS 3 lecture 'How the body clock works'. There are 5 sensory cranial nerves: olfactory, vestibulocochlear, optic, glossopharyngeal, trigeminal and the 3 motor cranial nerves: facial, glossopharyngeal, oculomotor. The remaining cranial nerves are both sensory and motor: hypoglossal and optic. Trochlea is not a cranial nerve. Note that the first sensory cranial nerve is olfactory, which is responsible for the specialised sense of smell. The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina to the brain. The other 3 sensory nerves all provide information about position and movement. The first 2 of these are the semicircular ducts, which are concerned with eye movements. The third is the vestibular nerve, which provides information about balance and spatial orientation. The glossopharyngeal nerve is one of the three motor nerves - it supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles and is responsible for the initiation of swallowing. The facial nerve supplies the stapedius muscle of the middle ear, and the cochlear division of the vestibular system. The oculomotor nerve is one of the four cranial nerves to supply muscles in the orbit. It supplies the superior, inferior and medial rectus muscles, and the inferior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CNIV). The remaining two cranial nerves are the trigeminal and hypoglossal. The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication (muscles of the temporomandibular joint) and the skin of the face. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic tongue muscles. Quinolones are used to treat bacterial infections. They are effective against infections caused by gram negative bacteria, which tend to be the ones involving the intracellular pathogen, Mycoplasma. They work by blocking the enzyme that usually causes unwinding of supercoiled bacterial DNA prior to replication, thereby preventing DNA replication. This leads to bacterial death. Quinolone antibiotics include Levofloxacin, Ofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin, and Moxifloxacin. Beta-lactams are used to treat infections caused by gram positive bacteria, such as staphylococcus. They work by interfering with the production of the bacterial cell wall. This leads to bacterial death. Baytril is an example of a beta-lactam antibiotic. Tetracyclines are used to treat a range of bacterial infections. They work by being taken up by the bacterium, and then acting by irreversible binding to the 30S subunit, preventing protein synthesis. An example tetracycline is Doxyclycline. Macrolides are used to treat infections of the upper respiratory tract. They work by inhibiting the translocation process within the 50S ribosomal subunit, leading to bacterial death. Azithromycin is an example of a macrolide antibiotic. Aminoglycosides are used to treat infections caused by gram negative bacteria. They work by blocking protein synthesis, by binding to the 30S subunit. An example of an aminoglycoside antibiotic is Gentamicin. Arteriosclerosis describes the hardening and thickening of the arterial walls resulting in a loss of their elastic properties Atherosclerosis is one of the processes that contributes to arteriosclerosis and involves the formation of an atheroma which is an accumulation of lipid plaques within the vessel wall. Although this process predisposes to a thrombotic event it itself refers to the plaque formation. Arteriosclerosis of the small arteries and arterioles is termed arteriolosclerosis and is mainly due to hypertension. Arteriosclerosis results in a reduced arterial lumen resulting in decreased tissue perfusion in addition to this due to the loss of elasticity rupture is increasingly likely to occur and there is a predisposition to thrombus formation. Atherosclerosis at the major vessel level often results in a thrombotic event and this results in tissue ischaemia and may result in necrosis. The plaque formation at these sites results in the vessel being occluded over 50% or more and so flow is greatly reduced and as a result of the loss of flow at the distal end there is a risk of tissue ischaemia. In atherosclerosis the arteries are not necessarily irregular in calibre but the plaque formation causes this effect. Arteriosclerosis is a chronic progressive disease with remodelling of the affected vessels while atherosclerosis is a degenerative disease with potential for sudden change from a stable plaque to an unstable plaque. The mechanism of Na+ reabsorption in the different parts of the nephron is as follows: PCT= The Na+/glucose symporter is used to absorb glucose and Na+ is absorbed passively by diffusion.Thick ascending limb= The Na+/Cl- transporter is used to absorb Na+ and 2Cl- are absorbed passively by diffusion.DCT= The Na+/Cl- co-transporter is used to absorb Na+ and Cl- is absorbed by active transport. The mechanism used in each part of the nephron ensures that the concentration gradient is maintained and that the highest concentration of Na+ is maintained within the filtrate. In the PCT, Na+ is passively diffused from the filtrate into the blood. In the thick ascending limb, Na+ is actively taken up into the blood by the Na+/K+2Cl- transporter. Cl- is also passively diffused from the filtrate into the blood in this part of the nephron. In the DCT, Na+ is actively taken up into the blood by the Na+/Cl- co-transporter. The high concentration of Cl- in the filtrate is used to drive the uptake of Na+. This ensures that the concentration gradient of Na+ is maintained so that all of the Na+ in the filtrate can be reabsorbed. Increased heart rate would cause positive inotrophic effect but this is not the predominant effect.  Atropine has an overall negative effect on the heart as it causes a reduction in the ability of the heart to contract. This is because atropine's action in the parasympathetic part of the ANS.  Muscarinic receptors are part of the parasympathetic ANS and as parasympathetic effects are overridden by sympathetic effects , atropine's overall effect on the heart is negative. The thalamus acts as the relay station for the stress response. It receives information from the sensory neurones, the amygdala (which detects emotion) and the hypothalamus (which controls the autonomic nervous system). It then relays this information to the appropriate part of the brain. For example, if the information is passed to the sympathetic branch of the ANS, it will trigger the release of norepinephrine and activation of the sympathetic nervous system. If the information is passed to the parasympathetic branch, acetylcholine is released and the parasympathetic nervous system is activated. Why these are incorrect:A - The thalamus does not process emotions. It receives information from the amygdala which detects emotion but does not process them itself.B - The thalamus detects when something is threating but it is not the first point of call. It receives information from the sensory neurones and the amygdala before making a decision.D - The thalamus is involved in relaying information. It does not dull the stress response.E - The thalamus receives information from the past in order to make a decision about what is happening in the present. This information is not accessed directly but rather is retrieved by the amygdala which then informs the thalamus. This is what allows the thalamus to make a decision about what is happening in the present based on past experiences. The glenoid labrum is the ring of cartilage surrounding the articular surface of the glenoid fossa. The glenoid labrum is the most lateral structure within the subglenoid capsule and is continuous with the intertubercular membrane at its inferior border. Its posterior portion is thicker and stronger than its anterior portion. The glenoid labrum is important for the stability of the shoulder joint. It prevents the glenoid labrum from being lacerated when the arm is dislocated. The glenoid labrum can be injured or worn away over time, which can lead to shoulder instability. Many procedures have been proposed for treating a damaged glenoid labrum, including open repair, arthroscopy, and bone-tendon-bone autografts.
